prompt:
A win-probability model for a competitive team video game is trained on
millions of historical matches, but the game receives balance patches
every few weeks that change the value of characters and items, so the
data-generating process is non-stationary. Retraining on recent data only
throws away useful history; training on everything lags after each patch.
Want a principled way to use all history while adapting fast after a patch.

Incorporate ideas from Animal and Plant Science Education (Social Sciences > Psychology > Social Psychology > Animal and Plant Science Education) into your approach.
proposal:
## The core tension

Full-history training gives you statistical power but lags behind every patch; recency-windowed training adapts fast but throws away signal that's still valid (matchup geometry, map structure, most of the roster that wasn't touched). What you actually want is a model that treats **most of the game as stable and a small, known subset as having just changed** — and updates its uncertainty about that subset accordingly. That framing turns out to map cleanly onto a handful of well-established ideas from evolutionary biology and quantitative genetics — the kind of material that shows up in animal/plant science education specifically because breeders and physiologists have been solving "how fast does a trait respond to a changed environment, using historical trials, without discarding prior generations' data" for over a century.

## 1. Decompose fast vs. slow components (phenotypic plasticity vs. genetic adaptation)

Biology distinguishes two response modes to an environmental shift: **plasticity** (a genotype rapidly expressing a different phenotype in a new environment, reversible, no selection needed) and **genetic adaptation** (allele frequencies shifting across generations, slow, needs many trials). Split your model the same way:

- **Slow/structural component** — matchup structure, map geometry, positional value, team-composition synergy: features that patches rarely touch and that should keep being estimated from *all* history.
- **Fast/patch-indexed component** — a per-character/per-item adjustment term, re-fit each patch, regularized toward its own history (random walk across patches, not i.i.d. per patch).

`win_prob = f(structural_features; θ_slow) + g(patch_features_t; θ_fast_t)`, with `θ_fast_t ~ N(θ_fast_{t-1}, τ²)`. This is a standard hierarchical/mixed-effects setup, but the biological framing is what tells you *where the split goes* — don't let the whole model drift; isolate drift to the part of the state space that's actually non-stationary.

## 2. Reaction norms from patch notes, not opaque per-patch embeddings

A **reaction norm** is the function mapping a genotype's phenotype across environments — measured in common-garden trials where the same genotypes are grown under different conditions to separate genetic from environmental effects. The equivalent move here: don't let the model learn "character X in patch 47" as a fresh categorical embedding that needs data to populate. Parse patch notes into structured numeric deltas (damage ±%, cooldown Δs, health Δ) and fit a **reaction-norm function** `stat_delta_vector → performance_delta` jointly across *all* historical patches.

This is the piece that actually solves your stated problem: the moment patch notes drop, before a single post-patch match exists, you get a zero-shot estimate of the win-rate shift from the historical relationship between numeric changes and their observed effects — the direct analogue of the breeder's equation, `R = h²S` (response to selection = heritability × selection differential), where "heritability" here is a learned transfer coefficient estimated from every previous patch's (stat change → win-rate change) pairs.

## 3. Shrinkage toward the reaction-norm prior (common-garden BLUPs)

For a genotype tested in only one or two field trials, breeding programs don't trust the raw trial mean — they compute a **BLUP** (best linear unbiased predictor) that shrinks the sparse observation toward the reaction-norm prediction, with the shrinkage weight determined by how much data exists. Same here: `θ_fast_t[character] ~ N(reaction_norm_prediction, τ²)`, and as post-patch matches accumulate, the posterior shifts smoothly from "reaction-norm prior" to "empirical patch data" — no hand-tuned recency window, no discontinuous retrain-vs-don't decision.

## 4. Patches as punctuated equilibrium, not continuous drift

Punctuated equilibrium (Eldredge & Gould) argues evolutionary change concentrates at speciation events, not steady background drift — long stasis, sharp jumps. A single exponential time-decay weighting treats the whole timeline as uniformly drifting, which is the wrong generative model here: it either overreacts to noise between patches or lags at the actual jump. Instead, treat patch timestamps as **known change points**: hold `θ_fast` fixed within a patch window, let it jump at patch boundaries, and only decay/reset at those boundaries. You have the true regime boundaries for free (patch dates) — use them instead of inferring drift statistically.

## 5. Self-tuning learning rate via associative-learning models (Rescorla–Wagner / Pearce–Hall)

For online updates between full hierarchical refits, classical-conditioning models from animal-learning research give you a mechanism, not just a metaphor. Rescorla–Wagner: `estimate_t = estimate_{t-1} + α·(outcome − predicted)`. Pearce–Hall extends this with an **adaptive associability**: α itself scales with the running average of unsigned prediction error, so learning speeds up exactly when the environment is surprising and slows down once it's predictable again. Implement this as your online updater between batch retrains: right after a patch, prediction errors spike automatically (the old model is wrong about the changed characters), α rises, adaptation accelerates; once the meta stabilizes, error shrinks and α decays. You get "fast after patch, stable otherwise" without ever explicitly detecting patch boundaries in this layer — it composes with the explicit change-point handling in #4 as a soft mechanism covering the interval between scheduled refits.

## 6. Inflate uncertainty post-patch, then let it settle (ecological succession / transplant shock)

After a disturbance, ecological succession runs through a high-variance pioneer stage before settling into a lower-variance climax community; transplanted organisms show an "acclimatization" or "transplant shock" period of elevated stress/variability before establishing. Concretely: multiply `τ²` for affected characters by a decay-from-high inflation factor triggered at each patch, decaying over the following ~1–2 weeks of matches. This isn't just cosmetic — it keeps the model's *calibration* honest (correctly wide confidence intervals immediately post-patch) even before enough data exists for shrinkage in #3 to narrow it naturally, which matters a lot for a win-probability model feeding downstream decisions (e.g., in-game odds, matchmaking).

## Putting it together

| Layer | Mechanism | Biology analogue | Solves |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feature split | slow structural + fast patch-indexed | plasticity vs. genetic adaptation | don't let whole model drift |
| Warm start | reaction-norm fit on patch-note deltas | reaction norm / common garden | zero-shot estimate at patch release |
| Regularization | BLUP-style shrinkage to reaction-norm prior | quantitative-genetics BLUPs | sparse post-patch data doesn't overfit |
| Segmentation | hard reset at known patch timestamps | punctuated equilibrium | avoids uniform-decay lag/overreaction tradeoff |
| Online updates | Pearce–Hall adaptive learning rate | associative learning / surprise-gated α | self-tuning speed without boundary detection |
| Calibration | variance inflation decaying post-patch | succession / transplant shock | honest uncertainty right after a patch |

Practically: retrain the full hierarchical model (slow features + reaction-norm layer) on a weekly-or-per-patch cadence using **all** history — nothing is discarded, because the reaction-norm layer is exactly what lets old patches keep contributing signal about *how* changes propagate to outcomes, not just *what* the outcomes were. Between refits, run the Pearce–Hall online updater per-character so live win-probability serving doesn't wait a full week to react.
